input:
Pervaporation is a membrane separation technique in which a liquid feed is brought into contact with one side of a membrane, while a vacuum applied on the other side draws the permeating component through the membrane in the form of vapour. In the present study, a polymer membrane and a zeolite membrane are compared in terms of flux, separation factor and stability for a single feed consisting of 85 wt% isopropanol in water at 60 °C. For clarity, flux is defined as the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1), while the separation factor is defined as the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the corresponding ratio in the feed, and is a dimensionless quantity.

The polymer membrane delivered a flux of 1.8 kg m-2 h-1 together with a separation factor of 180, whereas the zeolite membrane delivered a lower flux of 1.2 kg m-2 h-1 but a higher separation factor of 320. In terms of stability, however, the picture is reversed: the flux of the polymer membrane fell by 9% over 500 h, while the flux of the zeolite membrane remained unchanged over 500 h within the limits of measurement error. Taken together, these findings indicate that the polymer membrane leads in terms of flux, while the zeolite membrane leads in terms of separation factor and long-term stability over the duration of the test. It is important to note that no test was conducted beyond 500 h and that one feed composition was investigated, so the comparison is limited to 85 wt% isopropanol at 60 °C and to a maximum of 500 h of operation, the conditions under which flux, selectivity and stability were reported together for the same membrane.
target:
Pervaporation separates a liquid mixture through a membrane: the feed contacts one side of the membrane, and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. This study compares a polymer membrane and a zeolite membrane on flux, separation factor and stability for one feed, 85 wt% isopropanol in water at 60 °C. The comparison was made because flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1); the separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, and is dimensionless.

The polymer membrane gave a flux of 1.8 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 180. The zeolite membrane gave a flux of 1.2 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 320. On stability the order reverses: the polymer flux fell 9% over 500 h, and the zeolite flux was unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. The polymer membrane leads on flux, and the zeolite membrane leads on separation factor and on stability over the test duration. No test ran beyond 500 h, and one feed composition was tested: the comparison is limited to 85 wt% isopropanol at 60 °C and to 500 h of operation, the conditions under which flux, selectivity and stability were reported together for the same membrane.
